A modern system combines several layers with different capacities, latencies, and addressing rules. This note connects the pieces: SRAM and DRAM, CPU caches, segmentation, paging, multi-level page tables, and the translation lookaside buffer (TLB).</p><span id="more"></span><h2 id="SRAM-and-DRAM">SRAM and DRAM</h2><p>Static random-access memory (SRAM) is faster than dynamic random-access memory (DRAM), but it is also more expensive and less dense. That trade-off makes SRAM a good fit for small CPU caches such as L1, L2, and L3, while DRAM provides the larger main-memory pool.</p><p>The cache hierarchy works because programs tend to reuse recently accessed data and access nearby addresses. A small, fast layer can therefore hide much of the latency of a larger, slower layer.</p><h2 id="Cache-organization">Cache organization</h2><p>Most loads and stores pass through the cache hierarchy before reaching main memory. It is useful to keep instruction and data caches separate: code and data usually have different access patterns, and caching decoded instructions can avoid repeating front-end work.</p><h3 id="Processors-cores-and-threads">Processors, cores, and threads</h3><p>A physical processor is a CPU package. A processor can contain multiple cores, and a core can expose multiple hardware threads. Different cores have separate execution resources, while hardware threads on one core share those resources and are scheduled by the operating system.</p><p>The number of logical CPUs can be estimated Cores generally have private L1 caches, may share an L2 cache, and may share a larger L3 cache within a processor. Separate processors do not necessarily share any cache directly.</p><h3 id="Address-decomposition">Address decomposition</h3><p>A cache does not store a complete memory address in every line. It divides an address into an offset, an index, and a tag:</p><ul><li>The offset selects a byte within a cache line.</li><li>The index selects a set.</li><li>The tag identifies which memory region is a four-way set-associative cache, the index chooses one set and the tag is compared with the four tags in that set. This gives more placement flexibility than a direct-mapped cache without the cost of comparing every line in the cache.</p><h3 id="Cache-coherence">Cache coherence</h3><p>When multiple cores cache the same writable memory, they need a coherence protocol. A common write-invalidate design lets one core obtain ownership of a line for writing and causes other cached copies to become invalid. The next reader must then obtain the updated value. The exact protocol is hardware-specific, but the goal is the same: all cores must observe a coherent order of writes.</p><h2 id="Segmentation">Segmentation</h2><p>Segmentation divides a process address space into logical regions. Each segment has a base and a bound (or limit), and the hardware checks that a logical offset stays within the segment before forming a physical address.</p><p>The heap commonly grows from lower addresses toward higher addresses, while the stack grows in the opposite direction. resulting physical address is the base plus that checked offset.</p><p>An implementation can identify a segment explicitly, for example with selector bits, or implicitly from the pointer used to form the address. Segmentation can suffer from external fragmentation, so the operating system may need to compact or otherwise manage free regions carefully.</p><p>The allocator also needs to remember how large an allocation is when the caller later invokes <code>free(ptr)</code>. A common approach is to place a small header immediately before the user-visible payload. The header stores the size and allocator metadata, so the allocator can recover the chunk boundaries from the pointer alone.</p><h2 id="Paging">Paging</h2><p>Paging replaces variable-sized logical segments with fixed-size pages. A process's virtual address space is split into pages, and physical memory is split into same-sized frames. stretchy="false">(</mo><mtext>PFN</mtext><mo>,</mo><mtext> </mtext><mtext>offset</mtext><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>.</mo></math></mjx-assistive-mml></mjx-container> </span> <p>Page tables are normally per-process. The CPU keeps a pointer to the current process's page-table root, so the same virtual address can map to different physical frames in different processes.</p><h3 id="Multi-level-page-tables">Multi-level page tables</h3><p>A single, flat page table can be large even when a process uses only a small portion of its address space. A multi-level page table splits the virtual address into several indexes and one offset. Each index selects an entry in the next-level directory until the last level identifies the physical frame.</p><p>For example, a virtual address divided into four indexes and one offset uses a four-level page table. The extra levels add page-table walks on a miss, but they let the operating system allocate lower-level tables only for regions that are actually in use.</p><p>As the number of levels increases, a page-table walk becomes more expensive. That is why address translation is normally cached.</p><h3 id="A-large-page-example">A large-page example</h3><p>On a 32-bit machine using 4 MiB pages, the lower 22 bits are the page offset because xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><msup><mn>2</mn><mrow data-mjx-texclass="ORD"><mn>22</mn></mrow></msup><mo>=</mo><mn>4</mn></math></mjx-assistive-mml></mjx-container> </span> MiB. The upper 10 bits select one of the 1024 entries in the page directory. The selected entry supplies the physical page's base, which is combined with the 22-bit offset.</p><p>This is different from the more common 4 KiB two-level layout, where the address is split into a 10-bit page-directory index, a 10-bit page-table index, and a 12-bit offset.</p><h2 id="TLBs">TLBs</h2><p>The translation lookaside buffer is a small cache of recent VPN-to-PFN translations. On a TLB hit, the CPU can combine the cached PFN with the original offset immediately. On a miss, hardware or the operating system performs a page-table walk and then usually inserts the result into the TLB.</p><p>Without address-space tags, changing processes requires invalidating translations that belong to the old page table. Modern systems can use tags such as ASIDs or PCIDs to keep translations from different address spaces distinct and reduce the amount of flushing required during a context switch.</p><h2 id="Putting-it-together">Putting it together</h2><p>Caches optimize access to physical data. Paging translates virtual pages into physical frames, and the TLB caches those translations so that the translation step does not become the new bottleneck. Segmentation explains an older logical-address model, while paging provides the fixed-size mapping used by most modern operating systems.</p><p>The common theme is indirection with locality: keep the frequently used metadata and data close to the CPU, and use compact indexes to find the larger backing store only when necessary.</p><h2 id="Further-reading">Further reading</h2><ul><li><a href="https://people.freebsd.org/~lstewart/articles/cpumemory.pdf">CPU and Memory</a></li></ul>
entry.summary: A guided tour of the memory hierarchy, from SRAM and caches to paging, page tables, and the TLB.
entry.title: Memory Systems: From SRAM Caches to TLBs

Policy gradient methods take the more direct route: represent the policy itself with a neural network and adjust its parameters so that high-return actions become more likely.</p><p>This direct objective is attractive, especially for continuous actions, but it introduces a difficult estimation problem. A policy changes the distribution of entire trajectories, and the reward of one trajectory can be noisy. The policy gradient derivation explains both why the method works and why practical algorithms need variance reduction.</p><span id="more"></span><h2 parameters.</li></ol><p>The catch is variance. A single trajectory return is used to reinforce every action in that trajectory, even though early actions may have little connection to rewards received much later. Long horizons make this noise worse, so an unbiased estimator can still be too unreliable to train successfully.</p><h2 id="Causality-and-reward-to-go">Causality and reward-to-go</h2><p>An action at </span> <p>This product is the main problem. Even if each ratio is close to one, multiplying many ratios can produce extremely small or large weights. The estimator variance can grow rapidly with the horizon, making naive off-policy policy gradients unstable.</p><p>Trust region methods address this issue by restricting how far the new policy can move from the behavior policy. Another practical approximation uses state action marginals or clipped ratios instead of a full trajectory ratio. These ideas lead toward methods such as TRPO and PPO, where controlling policy change is as important as following the gradient.</p><h2 id="The-main-picture">The main picture</h2><p>Policy gradients optimize the policy directly through the distribution of trajectories. The log-derivative trick removes the need to know the environment dynamics, and REINFORCE turns the resulting expectation into a Monte Carlo update. Reward-to-go and baselines make the estimator less noisy, while a learned value function leads naturally to actor-critic algorithms.</p><p>The method is conceptually direct, not automatically low variance. Long trajectories, sparse rewards, and large policy changes can all make the gradient estimate unreliable. Good policy optimization is therefore a balance between a correct gradient objective and enough variance control to make that objective usable.</p>
entry.summary: A practical derivation of REINFORCE, reward-to-go, baselines, advantage estimates, and importance sampling.
entry.title: Policy Gradients: The Straightforward Route to Reinforcement Learning

The central question is simple: after reaching a state, how much future reward should we expect? The Bellman operator gives a principled answer, and value iteration repeatedly applies that operator until the estimate becomes consistent with its own one-step lookahead.</p><p>The tabular version is elegant, but it breaks down when the state is an image, a robot configuration, or any other high-dimensional continuous object. Fitted value iteration and fitted Q iteration keep the same Bellman idea while replacing the table with a function approximator.</p><span id="more"></span><h2 id="The-Bellman-optimality-operator">The enough</h2><p>A table works when the state space is small and discrete. It stores one number for every state, or one number for every state action pair in the case of a Q function. That representation becomes impractical as soon as the state is continuous or contains pixels. Two nearly identical images would also be treated as unrelated rows unless we build in some notion of similarity ourselves.</p><p>This is the curse of dimensionality. The number of possible states grows too quickly for a table to cover them, and visiting every state is impossible in many real environments. A neural network can share information across related states, but it also changes the convergence story.</p><h2 id="Fitted-value-iteration">Fitted value iteration</h2><p>Fitted value iteration keeps the Bellman backup and adds a regression step. The update resembles a gradient step because it moves the current estimate toward a target, but it is more precise to call it a stochastic approximation method. The target itself depends on the current Q function and on a random transition.</p><p>With a neural network, we can minimize a squared Bellman error with gradient descent. That optimization step is useful, but it does not turn the whole algorithm into ordinary supervised learning. The labels depend on a changing and sometimes unstable model, and the max operation can amplify estimation errors. Target networks, replay buffers, careful data coverage, and conservative optimization are practical ways to reduce those problems, not proofs that convergence is guaranteed.</p><h2 data-mjx-alternate="1">′</mo></msup><mo>,</mo><msup><mi>a</mi><mo data-mjx-alternate="1">′</mo></msup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>.</mo></math></mjx-assistive-mml></mjx-container> </span> <p>The behavior policy does not need to be the latest greedy policy. This is the meaning of off-policy learning: the policy producing the samples and the policy being evaluated or improved can differ. It is useful because old replay data can remain valuable while the estimated policy changes.</p><p>Off-policy does not mean that any data is sufficient. The replay set still needs enough coverage of useful states and actions. If the behavior policy never visits a region of the environment, the Q estimator has no reliable evidence there, no matter how many regression steps are applied.</p><h2 id="The-practical-picture">The practical picture</h2><p>The core loop is short:</p><ol><li>Collect transitions from an exploratory behavior policy.</li><li>Use the current value or Q estimator to build Bellman targets.</li><li>Fit the estimator to those targets.</li><li>Repeat while monitoring both prediction quality and environment returns.</li></ol><p>Tabular value iteration has a clean contraction argument. Once a neural approximator and a projection step are introduced, that argument no longer transfers automatically. The right mental model is therefore not that fitted value iteration is guaranteed gradient descent, but that it is repeated Bellman backup followed by approximate regression. It can work very well, but its stability depends on the function class, the data distribution, and the details of the training loop.</p>
entry.summary: A compact guide to Bellman backups, fitted Q iteration, function approximation, and off-policy learning.
entry.title: Q-Learning and Fitted Value Iteration
